title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
abstract: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes neural computation by treating measurement resolution as a critical variable, analogous to the coastline paradox. It develops an information-theoretic framework to decompose total predictive information into direct (pairwise) and higher-order components. The core finding is that the apparent complexity of neural processing is not fixed but critically depends on the specific scale or projection used for observation.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the apparent structure of neural computation changes depending on the observational resolution, drawing an analogy to the Mandelbrot coastline paradox.
main_result: The apparent interaction order and information content are highly dependent on the chosen measurement scale or projection map, meaning no single, scale-independent description of neural computation is uniquely determined.
method: It employs a scale-indexed information-theoretic decomposition, calculating measures like available information ($I_{avail}$) and direct information ($I_{dir}$) to quantify how much predictive power is captured by simple, pairwise models versus complex, higher-order interactions.
model_or_system: The analysis uses abstract statistical models applied to neuronal computation, considering dendritic cascades and synaptic inputs, often modeled with binary inputs and higher-order interaction laws.
key_observables: Available Information ($I_{avail}$), Direct Information ($I_{dir}$), Higher-Order Interaction Residual ($I_{higher}$), and the normalized direct fraction ($F$).
important_parameters: Observational resolution ($\epsilon$), projection map parameters ($\alpha, \Delta$), and the order of interaction (e.g., third-order coupling in the neuron model).
main_assumptions: The analysis is deliberately epistemic, treating the observed relationship as a projection rather than the true underlying physical law, and it notes that the point-neuron model is an abstraction, not the definitive reality.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how higher-order dependencies can appear pairwise after specific projections, and how the direct fraction ($F$) and available information ($I_{avail}$) change depending on the projection map used.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general concept of resolution dependence (coastline paradox) to a formal information-theoretic decomposition ($I_{avail} = I_{dir} + I_{higher}$), demonstrating this formalism using abstract spin systems and then applying it to detailed neuron models involving specific projections (symmetric vs. asymmetric maps).
why_interesting: While focused on neuroscience, the mathematical framework—using information theory to analyze how complexity is revealed or suppressed by measurement resolution—is highly relevant to understanding effective theories in complex many-body systems, such as those studied in disordered or correlated electron systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A higher-order dependency becomes pairwise after projection. (a) Exact enumeration at K = 1.8 gives 0.823 bits of connected third-order information at the fine scale and 0.261 bits of pairwise mutual information after the disjoint coincidence projection x = b1, z = b2 ∧b3. The projected variables are independent at K = 0. (b) The information that survives as pairwise depends on the map: an XNOR/parity projection retains all of I(3), whereas the coincidence map retains only part.

FIG. 2. Direct dependencies become more complete along an exact cascade. (a) Blue bars show F for the coordinate- invariant categorical-additive family; pink shows the residual share. Purple diamonds show the more restrictive linear-moment family, which yields 55.0%, 81.3% and 98.9%. (b) Coarse-graining reduces the available information Iavail, the captured direct information Idir and, more sharply, the conditional-KL residual Ihigher. Values are exact sums over all 64 input states.

FIG. 3. Organized multi-contact features improve held-out approximation. (a) Mean held-out MSE for a linear point neuron, a three-subunit model with shuffled contacts and a three-subunit model with contacts aligned to the target’s pair structure. Error bars are 95% normal intervals across 100 independent train–test trials (6,000 samples in each split). (b) Mean held-out MSE of a generic fixed sigmoid random-feature network. The first tested width whose mean reaches the aligned model is 40. Shading shows 95% normal intervals across 40 trials.

FIG. 4. Approximation and effective dimension grow in a nested hierarchy. (a) Mean held-out MSE as progressively more nonlinear sigma–pi subunits are exposed from the same architecture; the dashed line is the direct-input point baseline. Error bars and baseline shading are 95% normal intervals across 60 independent architectures and train–test sets (5,000 samples per split). (b) Normalized inverse error and normalized effective rank with log-space power-law fits. Exponent intervals are 95% percentile-bootstrap intervals over trials (2,000 resamples).
